---
title: "Theoretical Background"
---

The project relies on standard rigid body transforms between camera and
world frames. A point $p_c$ in camera coordinates is mapped to world
coordinates by an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ transform

$$p_w = R p_c + t,$$

where $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ describe the
camera pose. Homogeneous coordinates provide a compact representation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
p_w \\ 1
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
R & t \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
p_c \\ 1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Pixel coordinates $(u,v)$ with depth $d$ are converted to camera space by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix} = d
\begin{bmatrix}
(u-c_x)/f_x \\
(v-c_y)/f_y \\
1
\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $(f_x,f_y)$ and $(c_x,c_y)$ are the focal lengths and principal
point of the camera intrinsics matrix. The functions
`pixel_to_camera_coordinates` and `camera_to_world_coordinates` in
`aabb_segmentation.py` implement these equations.

The helper `compute_3d_center_from_bbox` samples depth values within the
2‑D bounding box, uses the median depth to mitigate outliers and then
projects the centre pixel into 3‑D. A similar routine
`compute_3d_center_from_mask` uses the centroid of a segmentation mask.

Given a 3‑D point $(x,z)$ in camera space the bearing in the bird's-eye
view is computed as

$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(x, z).$$

The angle is converted to degrees and mapped to a 12‑hour clock where
`0°` corresponds to `12 o'clock`. This is implemented in
`compute_rotation_from_3d_position`.
